questions.q: In an Apex test, what actually causes a queued event published inside `Test.startTest()`/`Test.stopTest()` to be delivered to its subscribers?
options: Calling EventBus.publish() alone delivers it immediately
Calling Test.stopTest() is what carries out the queued publish and delivers it to subscribers
Events are never delivered inside a test context
Delivery happens automatically one hour after the test method starts
questions.explain: EventBus.publish() only queues the event even in a test. Test.stopTest() is what actually carries out the publish and delivers it to subscribers on the test event bus.

questions.q: When would you need to call `Test.getEventBus().deliver()` explicitly rather than relying only on `Test.stopTest()`?
options: Never; stopTest() always handles every delivery scenario automatically
When a subscriber triggered by one event publishes a second event that also needs delivering, or when async Apex is involved
Only when testing a Change Data Capture event, never a custom platform event
Only when the event is standard-volume
questions.explain: Explicit deliver() calls are needed for chained publishes (a subscriber reacting to one event by publishing another) or when async jobs publish events that need their own delivery step.

The failure path of your publish-callback logic (onFailure), by forcing a publish to fail in the test
That Change Data Capture is enabled on an object
That an LWC component renders correctly on mobile
questions.explain: Test.getEventBus().fail() forces a simulated publish failure so a test can exercise EventPublishFailureCallback.onFailure() logic without needing a real production failure.

questions.q: Why is directly seeding a `Processed_Event__c` tracking row usually more practical than trying to force a real duplicate event delivery inside a test?
options: Because EventUuid is system-populated and not freely settable on a constructed event from Apex, making the tracking-check branch easier to test directly
Because duplicate delivery is impossible to test under any circumstances
Because Test.stopTest() automatically delivers every event exactly twice
Because idempotency logic cannot be unit tested at all
questions.explain: Since EventUuid is generated by the system rather than set by test code, testing the duplicate-skip logic directly against a pre-seeded tracking record is the practical approach, rather than trying to engineer a real redelivered duplicate.

questions.q: How does sfdx-lwc-jest let you test an LWC's `lightning/empApi` subscription logic?
options: By connecting the Jest test to a real Salesforce org's event bus
By providing a mock of the empApi module, letting a test manually trigger the mocked subscribe() callback with a fake message and assert the component's reaction
By disabling empApi entirely during tests
Jest tests cannot test any LWC that imports lightning/empApi
questions.explain: sfdx-lwc-jest mocks lightning/empApi so a component test can manually invoke the subscribed callback with a fake payload and assert the component's own reaction logic, without needing a real event bus connection.
